utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you also, during the course of your visit to Jablanica, you stayed there for about a day and that you visited front line units. How far were those units from the village?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact distance, but they had taken up defence positions that were outside the village, both on the left side and the right side. I can't tell you what the exact distance was, though, from the place where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you visited those front lines and then travelled from Jablanica, I think, to Gllogjan that evening; correct?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from there we went to Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you get from Jablanica to Gllogjan? Can I ask you the means that you used?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, we went there by vehicle, from Jablanica to Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you have to take any extra security precautions or did you just get into the car with your entourage and move from Jablanica to Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set off by car. Every one of us was armed, and we also had soldiers that escorted us. These were soldiers given to us by Ramush, and we went to Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So you had been provided with an escort by Mr. Haradinaj from at least the point that -- of time that you arrived in the area, namely at Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we left Jablanica there was an officer there, Salihu, but there were also soldiers that escorted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked questions by Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, and again it's just a very minor matter. You told us that the -- you were informed by the zone commander that the man called Togeri or Toger was Idriz Balaj. Again, can you tell us which individual you're talking about when you said that the zone commander identified him?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The zone commander, Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you said in evidence that -- this morning that Mr. Haradinaj introduced Toger and, as I understood your evidence, it was explained to you that he was experienced, that he'd fought in Croatia, and that he was a brave person. Is that -- do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And those features of Idriz Balaj, namely his experience, his past experience in Croatia, and his bravery, were matters explained to you by whom, by Mr. Haradinaj or by someone else?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haradinaj told you that?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you asked to be introduced to Toger or was that a matter that was raised with you in -- by others, by Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether there was a request to see him, but in the course of the tour I had I met him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned some names at the beginning of your cross-examination by Mr. Guy-Smith. Names were: Naim, Hazeri, Bekim Shyti, and Mensur Kosumi. As far as you were aware were all those men members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bekim Shyti had joined the KLA when we had the training. He was trained in the places where we conducted the training, while Mensur Kosumi was an officer in the Bosnian army and he participated in the Bosnian war and he was one of the officers that trained soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But what I -- the only real detail that I need is simply this: Those three men whose names I mentioned, were they at the time or did they subsequently become members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to turn now to your evidence that you gave yesterday in answer to questions by Mr. Emmerson. You were asked on three occasions about the absence of a building where KLA headquarters -- well, let me rephrase that. It was -- it was suggested to you, put to you, that there were -- and you were asked if the KLA had a building or headquarters in Tirana, and you said -- you said no. That was the effect of your evidence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know if that issue was ever discussed, the -- the acquisition of a permanent physical location for KLA headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know whether there was such a building in Tirana at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that -- evidence in chief, your evidence-in-chief, not in -- yesterday, in cross-examination, but evidence-in-chief, that the training you conducted had to be done clandestinely. What was the reason? Can I ask you if the reason for that would have applied to the setting up of any permanent physical headquarters in Tirana?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was because the Government of Albania did not allow us to operate in the Albanian territory. So by this, I mean to train our soldiers, the KLA soldiers, in their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand that. What I'm asking -- what I'm asking is this: Do you -- and tell us -- please tell us if you don't know. Okay? I'm not trying to make -- put words in your mouth, but tell -- make sure you tell us if you don't know, but tell us if you do know. Did that consideration also apply to the placing of a -- or the acquisition of, or the setting up of, a permanent building or structure for the KLA in that country, in Albania?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You were also asked questions by Mr. Emmerson concerning the movement of the General Staff within Kosovo, and you said in evidence: "The General Staff moved from place to place. They did not stay in one place only. Those movements were for reasons of security." And you touched upon this topic again this morning. What precisely -- what precisely did you -- was the reasoning behind moving the staff around and not keeping it in one particular building?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not receive any translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I can -- let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- if you would please repeat your question -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yeah, I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Di Fazio. And if you would like -- if you would please inform us if you still do not receive any translation. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yesterday you said, and again today you mentioned, that the General Staff moved around for reasons of security, and that was the reason why there wasn't a particular headquarters or one physical location. What precisely -- what was the thinking behind moving around from place to place?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned that the staff moved in -- into various areas because of security considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Let me put it to you this way: Was that -- was it -- were you concerned with the KLA General Staff being concentrated in one building or one location?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I speak of security considerations, I keep in mind the developments at the time. In July the Serb offensive started, so considerations of security became more important for the General Staff. But also, we couldn't stay in one place only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it might be obvious to you, but it's not quite obvious to me, and I would appreciate if you would spell it out as clearly as you can. You said it was important for the General Staff and that you couldn't stay in one place only. That's what you were being asked about in cross-examination. Now, why? Why couldn't you stay in one place only? Why not set up a headquarters in a village somewhere in Kosovo and stay there and operate out of that one building? Yeah?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to do that at that time because when I started in July until September/October, there were a lot of Serb offensives, and it was impossible for the General Staff to be located in a single facility. It was a matter of security and safety for its members. Many zones -- there were fightings in many zones, so it wasn't possible to be concentrated in one zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, thank you. You also were taken to the topic of communications between the General Staff and zone commanders, and you said in evidence -- or you agreed with the proposition that there were no regular communications, and that it was difficult to communicate. My question is: Was it possible to communicate at all? Did you sometimes achieve -- or did you sometimes communicate with the zone commanders?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my statement, from July that I was given this task in the operation department; and afterwards, the Serbs -- the Serb forces mounted attacks on us. Therefore, it was impossible to have frequent, regular contacts among the zone commanders or hold regular meetings. So, as I said, this made it impossible for the General Staff to hold regular meetings with the zone commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Do I -- can I take it from what you've just said that although it was impossible to have regular meetings and communications, there were communications of some sort from time to time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't receive translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Can you hear me now? Do you want me to repeat my question for you?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I had it translated again by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that we couldn't have frequent, regular contacts, but we did have some contacts, as the case was with my July visit in Dukagjin and in other zones which enabled me to meet the commanders and know the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And apart from personal visits, like the one that you have described at length, were there other means of communication, irregular and infrequent; for example, radio, or courier, or any other means of communication?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have radio communication, from what I remember, for the period I am testifying; that is, June, September, October. There were some instances of radio communication with some zones, but I, personally, I didn't have this kind of communication with the zones. Sometimes we used couriers; sometimes, depending on the situations, through direct contacts when we actually went -- physically went to the zones to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked by Mr. Emmerson this question and you provided this answer: "People would get together what scraps of uniform they could and any weapons they either had or could smuggle in from Albania and try to call themselves an army at this point?" You answered: "For that period, yes." Do you know where the weapons that were being smuggled in from Albania into Kosovo actually came from?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my information I got from other members, I know that they came from Albania, but I cannot give you information as to the precise source of such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You've -- you were asked again in cross-examination about - I think this morning - about your personal smuggling or transportation -- let's call it "transportation" of weapons into Kosovo. When you were based in Tirana and before the 28th of May when this happened, were you aware of other weapons being smuggled or transported from Albania and into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, I never thought that it was a kind of smuggling. I know that there was a logistical department which worked for that. I wouldn't call that smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't call it smuggling either; that's Mr. Emmerson's phrase. Let's call it "transportation." You've told us about your transporting weapons across the border into Kosovo; you did it personally on the 28th of May. My question is this: Did that phenomenon occur, as far as you're aware, prior to the 28th of May, when you were based in Tirana, in Albania?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Tirana, I know that there was a lot of transportation going on of weapons to Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know who was paying for those weapons?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I knew then, it was paid by the fund, "Vendlindja Therret"; that is, homeland is calling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And do you know who was making the decision to send that particular convoy or -- particular convoy across the border?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you accurate information, but I know that it was the duty of the logistical department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Of the KLA General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've told us -- you've touched upon what happened to the weapons that you took across on the 28th of May. Do you have any information as to what happened to the weapons that were transported across the border prior to that, the ones that you heard about that, that you had information about? Do you know how -- what happened to them once they got across the border and into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to them before the 28th of May. I only know that they were sent to Kosova, but as to what happened with these weapons after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Could the witness be shown P141.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's the document that was put to you by Mr. -- you were shown by Mr. Emmerson. MR. DI FAZIO: It's tab 4 in the Defence bundle, if Your Honours please. P141, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. You've got it up now. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you assist me, please. If you just run your eyes down through the document you'll get to a passage that would seem to be the words of Salih Veseli. Do you see that? Yes, I think you can see it on the first page. It might -- I don't know. I can't do the translation in my mind. The point that I am interested is, is these words. There seem to be the words: "Victory will not come from holding routes; this is fatal." Do you see those words? It might be the next page. See if you could -- I will be grateful if you could find that passage: "Victory will not come from holding routes; this is fatal." MR. DI FAZIO: It might be on the second page for all I know. Perhaps -- I think the witness has a hard copy there in front of him. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems he has. MR. DI FAZIO: I think he had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It's -- if I can assist you, it's -- you should see the name "Salih Veseli," and it starts off: "The people who are closest are those that understand one another. We have done something of great importance ..." Do you see it? And in the English, it would indicate that it's not very far into the document at all.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document, please? Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- the English that I've got here is -- it says this, and it's about ten or so lines under -- under the name "Salih Veseli." And then there's a notation: "Victory will not come from holding routes," then there is something illegible, and then the words "This is fatal." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found it? It's at the top of the second page. MR. DI FAZIO: If the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the semi-last -- just two lines above the separation line on the second page. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can deal with it this way. Perhaps I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where are we? We are, as a matter of fact, if I look at the screen, we are not -- yes. We are at the right place. Have you found -- it's approximately the third and fourth line from the top there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It says: "Victory will not come from holding" -- okay? It says -- you're looking at the part and it says: "Victory will not come from holding routes ... this is fatal." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just want to now take you to another passage in the -- in the document. I hope that you can just keep reading down slowly and it continues with the words of Mr. -- continuing R. Haradinaj and then Major Salih reading out something. And then Rrustem Teta speaking, Rrustem Teta. Do you see that passage where Rrustem Teta speaking?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And Rrustem Teta opined -- Rustem Teta says: "There's little consolidation of forces. There's no excuse for self-satisfaction with what has been done. I cannot call our territory a free zone while the enemy holds the road routes and towns." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just following --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during your visit in July to the area and when you met with these men, these local soldiers, did anyone express those sentiments to you that: "Victory will not be achieved by holding the routes," and that: "The territory could not be called a free zone while the enemy," presumably the Serbs, "hold the roads and towns"?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during my visit, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time that you visited in July -- July, the Serbs held the main road that you crossed to get to Reka e Keqe, at least they had positions on there that caused you to go -- to take security precautions; correct?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes. When I went to Reka e Keqe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. You've told us all about that, how you had to cross the road at night and so on. And as far as you're aware, did the Serbs also hold the big towns of the local towns in the area?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all the cities were under the control of the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Before we go to a different document, may I ask for precision because the translation is not complete in regard of this sentence with holding the routes or holding routes. There is some -- some place named illegible, called illegible. MR. DI FAZIO: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Now, this is -- and now you also cited it in a slightly different way. So can we go up once more to that place where victory is not -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be the top of page 2. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, would you go back to that -- to that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: To check that sentence. MR. DI FAZIO: Did Your Honour want me to do that or did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, maybe the witness could explain to you, yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, firstly, read it out as best you can, that -- that sentence: "Victory will not come ..." read out in Albanian what you can read, please.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Freedom cannot be won by holding scientific directions." This is what it says here. I don't know what he has meant by this word. From the military point of view, it means that someone is engaging in mil -- in science and not in concrete works. Personally, I don't understand this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Verification will be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm receiving some indications from behind that there is a problem with the translation of that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, I also had the impression. MR. DI FAZIO: That's precisely why I asked the witness to read it into the transcript and to get the -- the court interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just so that we're absolutely certain, read it out carefully, the words that appear in that phrase. Read them out in Albanian and clearly, so that the interpreters can hear them, and include at the end of it anything referring to the word "fatal."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, if Mr. Willemsen could be excused from the court proceedings for but a moment, I know that you have to walk through, so that we can also have it independently double-checked right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please slowly read the sentence, Mr. Zyrapi, to the best of your ability in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even though the handwriting is very poor to -- "You cannot win by -- by holding scientific directions; this is fatal -- fatal." Full stop. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- before you came to the -- MR. DI FAZIO: Firstly, does that satisfy Your Honours' concerns or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, it gives us some information. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Yes. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Up until you came to The Hague, had you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them -- you think now? During the time I'm here or --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, no. What I mean is up until recent months, had you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't see this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And it would seem on the face of it that it was created on the 23rd of June, 1998, and that was before you went to -- to the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to object to the question just posed unless Mr. Di Fazio is now going to be testifying because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I think the -- there was quite a -- it was elicited several times that the 23rd of June was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not dis -- that I'm not disagreeing --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now -- and then the second -- I'm just trying to analyse the whole of it. And then that was before you went to the area, I think "the area," need to be further defined in order not to have any -- MR. DI FAZIO: Dukagjini, I meant Dukagjini, the Dukagjini area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's also the previous question, which is posed by Mr. Di Fazio, in which is: "What I mean is up until recent months, had you seen this document before?" And that's a vague question and, I think, somewhat confusing in the context of what the witness is testifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, you'd like to have more precision, that's fine. Mr. Emmerson, you're on your feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: My concern also related to that first question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's ask the witness, let's keep matters clear. When did you for the first time see the document, Mr. Zyrapi, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the microphones is switched off. Could you please switch the other microphone on -- no, it's -- Yes. When did you, for the first time, see the document which you find now on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this document here when the Prosecutor showed it to me as a document, but not before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was, well, let's say, when you arrived in The Hague this month? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that satisfy --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, just to be clear, we obviously have a record in the witness's statement of the documents that have been shown to him and the documents that are produced. Now, Your Honours may recall that when I dealt with this document in cross-examination, I pulled up on the screen a much fuller minute of the same meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- which is unquestionably in the Prosecution's documents that were shown and purportedly exhibited by this witness. So there is -- he has been shown and has identified in some detail the full narrative minute of the meeting in which a lot of this material is recorded in greater detail. As far as this document is concerned, obviously we'll all check the records, certainly it was my recollection that this, too, had been shown to the witness and that he had produced it. But if I'm wrong about that, I will correct it. But I'm certain, or as certain as I can be, that the document that was pulled up on the screen, which relates to the same meeting and is a much fuller minute of it, is one which he commented on in some detail in his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that in any way contradict the answer of the witness? MR. DI FAZIO: No, it doesn't. I'm grateful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Answer of the witness -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- it will save me some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand the -- where the witness commented, we are talking about the April statements, April 2007? MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be fully in line with what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm not -- I'm not questioning that. I simply wanted to make it absolutely clear that when we dealt with this in cross-examination, I indicated to Your Honours and pulled up on the screen the much fuller record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Mr. Emmerson, that's -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's exactly what I'm trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no problem with that. I think -- don't think it needed this intervention because, of course, we make a distinction between document A and document B, even if it's -- relates to the same event. Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you were asked in detail by Mr. Emmerson about the contents of this document, and you were asked this series of questions and you gave this series of answers, and this is at page -- I'm sorry, I've only got page 69 -- oh, no, it's 3325.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise, I know I -- I know Your Honours already indicated that you thought my last intervention unhelpful, but I'm looking at page 13 of the witness statement of the 12th of April, and the very document that is on the screen is produced by the witness in that statement. So that much, I hope, is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were asked this series of questions, you gave this series of answers: "It says subsequently at a question by Ramush -- Salih Veseli and give" -- I'm sorry, this is not very clear English, but I'll do my best. "... and give a professional clarification of the tasks of a commander, the deputy, and Chief of Staff. Do you see that? "A. Yes. "Q. So it's clear, is it not, that this was a process of election, first of all. Do you agree with that? "A. Yes. "Q. Attended by villages which had been operating autonomously up until then but are trying to come together in a single command? "A. Yes. "Q. It culminates in a vote in favour of Ramush Haradinaj as the commander; correct? "A. Yes. "Q. At which point he immediately turns to one person who has military experience and asks him, What should a commander do? What should the roles and responsibilities be? "A. Yes." Were you agreeing with all of those propositions on the basis of something that you knew, something that you'd been told, or were you simply agreeing that that's what the document says?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was agreeing to the words of the document, because I wasn't present at this meeting to know what was discussed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hoepfel has one or more questions for you, Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zyrapi, please, I would like to ask you some questions about the weapons again, but as to the purchasing of which you were involved in Albania during the first period of time until 28th of May. So you might be able to give us some more details. First: Where, to which dealers, would you go to inspect and buy this weaponry?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I worked in close cooperation with a logistics department, people like Raif Gashi, Ilir Konushefci, and so on, and with these people I went to inspect the weapons technically, and whether these weapons could be bought or not. I don't know who the dealers were, who people -- who the people who were selling these weapons were. It was just that I gave my approval, technical approval, that these weapons could be used. I don't know what the logistics department did with regard to the purchasing of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. And what can you say about the origin of this material, both weapons, even if old weapons, and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons I inspected were old weapons, Chinese make. Some of them were also produced in Albania, some were Yugoslav weapons. These were the weapons that I saw at the time when I inspected them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And as to the authorisation for ordering or purchasing these weapons, I take it that the logistics department was in charge of that. But do you know, did they have a sort of a limit in terms of the price or -- amount of weapons to buy or who was in charge of those questions?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware about any of those things. I was not part of the negotiations or establishing the price or things like that. Those were decisions that were, of course, taken by the logistics department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zyrapi, quite a few questions have been put to you in relation to the 23rd of June meeting where, as we saw on the document, it was decided who would be in command of the Dukagjini Zone. Do you have any knowledge of whether the Dukagjin Zone command exercised at any earlier stage any authority or any power in an area other than just the limited Dukagjin Zone? I mean to that, the zone east of the road you described, the Decani-Djakovica road. So the question is whether any authority or any power was exercised outside that area, especially west of that road, prior to the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that. I wasn't in the area, so I don't know who exercised control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you also don't know whether actually on the 23rd of June this -- well, let's say this unified command of the Dukagjin Zone was established or other -- or whether it existed already before that date?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know whether it existed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified that no one in the KLA received any salaries throughout. How would people feed their families or -- I mean, how could people survive without any payment; do you know?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak of each and every case in particular, but I know that there were no salaries in the KLA in general. I have to say, though, that the people of Kosovo helped us with food and clothes and helped the families. I don't know how the families managed, but we were accommodated by the people and we were helped by the people all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We have seen - let me just have a look at it. We have seen a document -- perhaps it can be shown to the witness P153. Yes. Could we please -- have you ever seen that document before, Mr. Zyrapi?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a programme - at least that is what it says - for the training for units. We looked at it and we see a lot of subjects being part of that training. You were involved in training units as well or in preparing for the training of units?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also had that task at the time, but I had never seen this document before. It looks like a document that represents the plan for the training of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, looking at this programme - and I'm not asking you to focus on this programme - but I saw there was no training -- at least, it doesn't appear on the document, there was no training in international humanitarian law, that is to say, what is allowed and what is not allowed during warfare or during armed conflict. Was that ever any part of a training programme you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I recall, I'm not sure whether in the beginning they did such training, but from November onwards when I was Chief of Staff and organised trainings for commanding officers, from the level of the company and the battalion, this was included into the training. But earlier than that, I don't know. However, according to the information I had from the former director of the operational department, he told me that he had prepared a brochure that he had distributed to the units on the ground. It was like a booklet. I don't know what else was done. As I said, this was a very dynamic period. I was moving all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Finally I'd like to ask you whether -- whether there was any structure of military court, any structure to investigate and prosecute any crimes that might have been committed?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, until December 1998, there wasn't any military court; then, with the organisation of the staff, one was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you have any recollection of cases that were brought before that court?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but there were cases of breaches of the rule book of the KLA. The court was something that was controlled by another department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us anything about the breaches? What kind of breaches? Could be of all kinds?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I speak of breaches, I speak of military breaches committed by the soldiers or the officers of the KLA, meaning breaches of the provisional rule book of the KLA, such as, for example, mistakes made by soldiers who have been sent to this court in order for that kind of mistake or error to be evaluated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mistake or error. Was there ever a case heard on crimes committed against non-KLA army members, from what you remember, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember of any such case. There might have been, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever become aware of the Serb police recovering a number of corpses in September 1998 in the Dukagjin Zone?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any information to that effect at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did you then learn that, if you say "at the time," or did you ever learn it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on I heard when the trial started, this case started. I heard that it was part of the indictment against Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. If you would find in a document of the operational headquarters of the Plain of Dukagjin of mid-July that instructions are given and if these instructions are violated, that those who are violating this order might be brought to a military court - I'm talking about mid-June 1998 - what would be your comment in relation to your answer that a military court was established only five, six months later?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, during that period there was no court, but there was no request as well during that time about any such breaches in the Dukagjin area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if you tell your subordinates that they'll be brought before a military court, if it doesn't exist, that at least surprises me. Therefore, I'm asking you whether there was any structure already in July in place that could investigate or before which one could prosecute those who did not obey orders?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we're talking about the period when the court did not exist, and I don't know how they dealt with these issues and if they dealt with those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss that when -- in mid-July, when you visited the Dukagjin Zone, setting up courts or ...?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I recall, we did not discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got no further questions. Have the questions of the Bench triggered any need for further questions to the witness? If not, then this concludes your evidence, Mr. Zyrapi, in this courtroom. May I take it that the presence of Mr. Zyrapi is not needed to further discuss the admission of -- of the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think I've communicated to the Prosecution the areas of difficulty, and I think Mr. Di Fazio would like a little longer to assimilate and respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But the presence of the witness is not needed? MR. DI FAZIO: No, we don't need him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that's right. And whilst I'm on my feet, may I apologise. I misspoke myself earlier on. It is correct that both of those two minutes are referred to in the April statement, but it's also correct, and Your Honours have it, that in the 2005 statement the typed minute is also referred to and commented upon at paragraph 31 and exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we clarify one thing as to these two minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the witness or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we can use the witness in this regard, because, Mr. Emmerson, you pointed out you identified this as two minutes of one and the same meeting. Do I remember correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But would you characterise them when -- when tendering them as -- with the dates, because they have two different dates actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think they, in fact, bear the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The date is at the end of the typed minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- 24th, and the first one is 23rd, actually. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I think -- I think there is some confusion. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- the document that is the same minute is not in the printed bundle, it was the one that I brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Oh, yes, now I see. And these are --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that is -- if Your Honours look to the -- to the statement of November 2005 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- the penultimate document attached -- in the redacted version that was admitted, 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The penultimate document in that bundle -- there's a single sheet at the end, which relates -- which is a different order, and then immediately before that, there is a document that begins on -- if one looks at the numbers in the top right-hand corner, 0 -- so U0091350 through to 1353. Now, that is the document that I brought up on the screen yesterday but which is not in the yellow file. It's referred to at paragraph 31 of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and it is the 23rd of June typed minutes of the same meeting, and it's possible literally to trace through speaker by speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't that the document for which there was no translation available?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, there was a translation available, it was on the screen yesterday, we looked at it in the course of the evidence, and it's Exhibit P142.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It may be very helpful because it is, as I say, a much more detailed narrative account of that very same meeting, but it follows literally speaker by speaker, and that is the one which this witness looked at in November 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. There was no translation available as an attachment to the statement. There --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But P1 -- is that -- I yesterday expressed some concerns about an original English statement with attachments which were - at least in hard copy - in Albanian, though not translation, and then I checked in the system, and I think I made reference to a 26- or a 25-page document and a 15-page document. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the translation was -- has the translation now been added? MR. DI FAZIO: It was added to the original version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was added to the original version, which is the English version. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, to the original statement, to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the statement in the -- in Albanian? MR. DI FAZIO: In English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, that is not this document; that's a different document. The document that we're dealing with here, P142 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it seems to have the -- I look at the attachment to the November 2005 statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where I find something which is called "Proces Verbal," that's the major title.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the very bottom it says: "The 23rd of June, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And from what I remember, it also -- ERN numbers went up to U0091353, and I think I heard you use that same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then -- it is appended to the statement there. So it's U0091350 to 1353 in the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And it is now Exhibit P142 in the system. I pulled it up yesterday with its translation which is linked. And indeed Your Honour asked some questions about the translation, because if you remember in the rough minute the remark from Nazmi Brahimaj is -- it is a done deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and in the complete minute, it is a fait accompli or the other way around. So, one can trace the two documents through the one to the other, they're exactly the same meeting, the same minute. It's just that this is much more detailed than the rough one, but the rough one appears to have been the notes that were to be taken, so to speak, simultaneously as the meeting was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, and clearly it was not necessary anymore, to have the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Before the witness is asked to leave, Your Honour, Judge Orie, you had asked the witness a number of questions concerning military discipline, military courts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- matters of that nature. I wouldn't seek to take the witness to it if we're all on the same page, and the page that I'm thinking of is the witness's statement from -- I think it's July of 2006, the 6th of July, 2006, at page 7 and 8, where he deals in some detail in paragraphs 25 onwards in that statement with his understanding of when those structures were first established. And that would mean, in fact, that none of those structures, military discipline structures, were in existence to his knowledge prior to him becoming Chief of Staff in November of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. But July 2006 statement is not admitted into evidence. It's not tendered. It's -- I think only the November 2005 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the April 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Exactly. It's for that reason that I'm on my feet, and it might be appropriate to ask the witness to just read those I think four paragraphs to himself and confirm the accuracy of the contents of those four paragraphs, if Your Honour thinks that that would be helpful to the Tribunal's understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- I asked the witness about it. He said something about it. I'm not seeking at this moment further details, but if the parties consider it important for us to have that -- but then which paragraphs would you then specifically -- because we might then consider to -- you said 25 starts with --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think 25, 26, 27, 28 -- I think those are fairly comprehensive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- in response to the issues that Your Honour was raising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps for completeness sake it might be good. Do we have an Albanian copy of this statement that could be given to -- because I've got here the -- I've got only the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, I too have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any Albanian copy available? MR. DI FAZIO: Regrettably, no. I don't have an Albanian copy -- hard copy here with me. I'm just wondering if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you find one soon or is there any way --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The shorter way might be simply for me to read it or Your Honour to read it in English to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I could read it to the witness--

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Otherwise we'll spend a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and try and keep a pace that can be followed by the interprets. Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, there's one issue in relation to some questions I have put to you. You gave a statement in July of 2006. I will read a portion of that statement to you, and I would like to invite you to carefully listen because at the end I'll ask you whether this reflects what you said at the time and whether, if you would be asked the same questions, whether you'd give the same answers. I'll slowly read it -- yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It also can be found in e-court. It's 2D250090.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In Albanian. Then let me slowly read it and if it could be shown on the screen then it might assist the witness. "Discipline issues did arise within the zones. Zone commanders had authority to summarily deal with minor breaches of military conduct with recourse to the General Staff or military court. Punishment could range from a verbal or written admonishment to detention for a short period of time. The zone commanders would include such action in their regular reports to the General Staff" --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just pausing there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour read "with recourse to the General Staff" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Without recourse." If I read that -- if I made a mistake, then I'll read that line again. "Zone commanders had authority to summarily deal with minor breaches of military conduct without recourse to the General Staff or military court." And then it continues that: "The range was from verbal or written admonishment to detention for a short period of time. The zone commanders would include such action in their regular reports to the General Staff. "In more serious cases the zone commanders would immediately detain offenders and the case would be referred to the military court. Until my appointment to Chief of Staff, the General Staff had not really issued orders regarding disciplinary matters. The decisions on issues concerning detaining persons, seizing vehicles and other property, and even just stopping people in the operational areas had really been in the hands of the zone commanders. "During August and September of 1998, I heard complaints about soldiers misusing their power when I visited the local commanders in the zones. There was an obvious need to have orders issued about this in order to be able to take disciplinary action against soldiers, but also for the soldiers to know what the right procedures were. The KLA operated according to the rule book of the General Staff of the KLA and the internal rule book of the KLA. These were printed booklets which regulated the activities of the General Staff, and everyone that come under their authority. "I'm unable to speak authoritatively regarding the compilation and publishing of these books, but I assume that much of what was contained within them was borrowed from rules already established by Western armies. Many copies of the rule books were produced and distributed among all seven zones. The zones were then responsible for the distribution of the books within their area of responsibility. Based upon the rule books, the commander of the General Staff or myself would issue orders and directives aimed at clarifying the action to be taken in specific circumstances. Orders in relation to operational and military matters were exclusively my responsibility, although I would also issue orders in relation to other areas of the rule books."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Might I suggest that the following paragraph should also be read to the witness or at least the material part of it. Paragraph 14 at page 4, which begins: "In November 1998, I was appointed as the Chief of Staff of the KLA General Staff. The composition of the General Staff was not at that time significantly different from its composition as at January 1999. This being," and then he lists himself, of course, and others. And he then lists military court Sokol Dobruna, just indicating that all of this is as of November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before we go on to another passage in the witness statement, I'm concerned about the way this matter has been introduced, at this stage what amounts to a Rule 92 ter excerpt in circumstances where it is possible that there could be a lack of clarity about dates. My understanding of the witness's evidence is that everything that is contained in paragraphs 25 to 28 relates to events that occurred after he became Chief of General Staff in November of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask the witness whether what was just read relates to -- let's first ask the witness. I read a portion of your statement; Mr. Harvey added some to it. Does this reflect what you said when this statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you -- if you would be asked about it at this moment, would you give the same answers as you gave at the time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would give the same answers. This is my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when I read the portions about the discipline issues arising and whether the commanders could deal with it without recourse to the General Staff or military court, what time were you then talking about, what time-frame?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period from November 1998 onwards, the period when I was Chief of Staff. So the period is from November onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in that statement, there's also a line which says: "During August and September of 1998, I heard complaints about soldiers misusing their power when I visited the local commanders in the zones. There was an obvious need to have orders issued." May I then take it that you earlier became aware, but that all the measures put in place, that is, the rule book, et cetera, that that was on from the moment that you became Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the period of August when I visited. There were irregularities at that time, and commanders in September, for example, complained about some soldiers misusing their powers. So on the basis of the requests made by commanders when I received the duty of Chief of Staff, I issued the order for this. But you should remember that the time, August, September, and so on, it was a period of -- of very intensive fighting of Serb offensives. So we couldn't do anything at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any need for further -- Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if there's any -- any need for further discussion. I'm just a little bit concerned because of the manner in which this has come in, we may be endeavouring to put a square peg into a round hole. And I had stopped earlier from asking a question with regard to the issue of why not set up headquarters in a place. But I think -- I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, matter of fact, I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- the reason -- the reason I'm raising it, Your Honour, is because I think that it's been pretty well established that during the period that we are dealing with here, and that is from the beginning of the year up until September, it was a fledgling army that had no radio communication, that had insufficient weapons, with a fleeing population, there was no secure area that realistically could be held and they were fighting for survival --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- and the reason I'm raising it is because of concerns that exist for the additional protocol II as the court has now dealt with the issue of the potential of having some form of military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll say a few words about it, but does it trigger any need for further questions? If not, then I'd like first to excuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's just one matter I wish to raise with Your Honours, and it relates to Judge Hoepfel's question about the passage in the minute that was illegible, and there was some concern with the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's a matter for Your Honours to decide, having heard the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In the fuller minute, the same passage which is referred to in the draft minute as being the speech of Salih Veseli is given the name Majori, but it's the same text, and the translation for that passage reads: "One cannot win by defending directions; this is deadly." So the translation -- the official translation of the official minute is: "One cannot win by defending directions; this is deadly." That was the passage that Mr. Di Fazio re-examined on and that Judge Hoepfel was particularly interested in the translation of. So I don't know whether anybody wants to take that further. If so, it's P142.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Zyrapi, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague, and I wish you a safe trip home. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to make one short comment on the development of the procedure over the last couple of minutes. I put a few questions to the witness on a matter which, at least, is not in evidence on the basis of the July 2006 document. I focused my questions on July; of course I did that because there is one of the documents in the bundle says something about, If you violate this order, I'll send you to a military court. Now, that was the only thing that happened. I was a bit surprised that if then my attention is drawn and we read into the record a lot of evidence I was not specifically seeking at that time, and then to be later confronted with all the problems that reading into the record would create. That is the world upside down. I just wanted to tell you this, that, Mr. Harvey -- I'm not looking at anyone specifically, but you're on your feet. I don't want to have long debates on the matter, but just to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I apologise. I -- I was a little more concerned than I think it actually made sense for me to be, in retrospect, and I think it was probably unnecessary to perform that exercise. But I just wanted a little clarification as to dates and times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since you're a bit the victim now, I'd like to make one further observation. When I put questions to the witness on decision-making on the 23rd of June and whether then the unified command was created, Mr. Emmerson asked the witness to take his earphones off and then started explaining to me what we find in the pre-trial brief. It may be clear that my questions were related to a 15th of June document which we find among the material from outside -- well, let's say west of the road, where it clearly says it's on the order of the Dukagjin command, it says that people could move around only with the consent of the Dukagjin command and the local commander. And that was the document which is a document of an area which is clearly outside -- so that was the basis of my questions. And next time, Mr. Emmerson, you are invited to further reflect before you start explaining to me what the Defence case is because the Defence case is not, as such, binding or guiding to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. And I want to apologise if I may for the tones in which I raised that. I had misunderstood the purpose of Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I thought Your Honour was suggesting from the comment by Nazmi Brahimaj which I thought Your Honour had connected that to that the minutes of the 23rd of June meeting were an indication that the Dukagjini staff were seeking to exert control through a fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least the document of the 15th of June leaves some questions open. I was exploring those --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even without being reminded to what the pre-trial brief says -- it's accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break for 20 minutes. We'll resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson, before I give you the floor, the Chamber is aware that a new issue has arisen, that's -- that's of course the risk of sending now and then copies to our legal staff, then the legal staff will inform us to the extent relevant, that a new issue has been arisen about notes or witness -- Witness 29, as we understand, recently has given to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have been disclosed. The Chamber wonders whether it makes sense at this moment to deal with the issue if we have not yet further information which I understand will be elicited from the witness anyhow by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the Chamber would prefer to deal with the matter once we have learnt more about the notes, whether it's a diary, whether it's -- whether the remainder is relevant for us, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I address Your Honours briefly in private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I will deliver the reasons for the decision on protective measures for Witness 29. Yesterday, on the 24th of April, upon hearing that the Defence was not opposing, the Chamber orally granted the Prosecution's motion of the 23rd of April, allowing Witness 29 to retain his earlier granted pseudonym and, as well, granting him face and voice distortion. The reasons for granting the motion are as follows: As the Chamber has stated on prior occasions, the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or his family should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. In the present case, the witness has been subjected to threats on a number of occasions and has had his property attacked several times, while some of the persons with whom the witness was closely associated during the period listed in the indictment have been assassinated. Moreover, the witness has moved out of Kosovo for security reasons and continues to fear for his safety and the safety of his family members. The Chamber, therefore, finds that there is a risk that if the identity of the witness were to be made public, physical harm might result to the witness or the witness's family. And this concludes the Chamber's reason for its grant of protective measures of Witness 29. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I inquire whether Your Honour has it in mind to hear further submissions in relation to the subpoena once the factual foundation has been established or to hear the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Depends. It depends -- it depends on what the factual foundation brings us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the face and voice distortion in place effective? Then, Mr. Kearney, I take it you would now like to call your next witness, being Witness 29. But we first turn into -- no, we don't have to turn into private session. Madam Usher, could you please escort Witness 29 into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness 29. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 29, because that's how I will call you, you are testifying under pseudonym. We'll not use your own name. Before you give evidence in this court, you are required to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Please be seated. Witness 29, you'll be first examined by Mr. Kearney, who's counsel for the Prosecution. And don't be surprised if -- especially in the beginning of the examination, the focus will very much be on the notes you have written in the past. Mr. Kearney, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the outset, I would like to call up, if I may, 65 ter document 1313; this is the personal data page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which should not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, can you see that document on the screen before you, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you please read the information on that document and tell us if it's accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That is your name and your -- your date of birth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P262, marked for identification and under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that there will be no objections. The document is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I'm going to ask Madam Usher, if I may, to deliver this booklet to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, I'd like to have you take a look, please, at that notebook and ask you if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes, this is my notebook. I recognise it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And is that a notebook you brought with you to The Hague when you arrived, this week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: There is writing on some of the pages inside that book, is there not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Is that writing in your hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, I'd like to ask you first: When did you buy that book? When did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: I bought this notebook a month and a half before coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: So you bought that notebook in calendar year 2007; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know the exact date, just approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: We're going to talk more specifically in a moment, but just in a general sense, can you tell us, please, what it is you wrote in that book? What was your -- the words you wrote, what were you attempting to record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: My aim was to write here all the notes that I had written during the war in pieces of paper. I wanted all of those notes to be in this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And we'll talk about those in a moment. Besides transcribing those notes you just mentioned, did you write other data in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: I also have some others, but here I only have this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Maybe I should -- I'll back up a question. You said that in that notebook, you transcribed original notes from calendar year 1998. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Those original notes from 1998, describe those for us, please. What were they that -- the items that you re-transcribed into this notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Notes on the events that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Those original notes, when were they made in relation to the events that you were describing in the notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: I always made those notes the same day the event happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And those original notes in 1998, what did you -- what did you write them on initially? What kind of paper did you record those -- those notes on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Different pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you still have those different pieces of paper that you recorded the original notes on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Some of them still exist; some of them I have lost, unfortunately. But most of them I think still do exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Those original notes that still do exist, where are they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Some of them are at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This is not your -- when you say your home, not the -- the place where you're staying in The Hague but the place you came from. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Is there a way -- would there be a way for you to have those faxed here to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: No, because for the moment I'm living in two different countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, could you explore - the witness said that "some of them are at home" - where the others are?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, you indicated that some of the notes are at home. Where are the rest of the notes? Are they -- where is the remainder of the notes that are not at home, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: The rest that are not at home -- I mean, some of the things that I transcribed on this notebook, some of them I kept and some I tore up. I didn't think they were useful or they were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Have you already given to the Office of the Prosecution a number of your original notes relating to events that took place in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes, I did hand them over, some of them, but not now, earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How many notes are still remaining in your home that you have not turned over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Is there a reason, Witness 29, that you did not bring the original notes with you here to The Hague, but rather transcribed those notes into the notebook you have before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: There is no specific reason, just that there were only bits and pieces, scraps of paper, and I didn't think it reasonable to bring those. There were cases that on one scrap of paper I had several notes, and, as I said, these were scraps of paper. I sometimes even found a piece of paper on the ground somewhere and wrote on it. And that's why I thought it wasn't necessary to bring those here, and that's why I transcribed everything on this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you transcribed this information into your notebook, did you do that accurately? Did you change anything from the original notes that you -- you made the notes on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Everything was as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In the notebook before you, are there notations about calendar years beyond 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Mainly these notes concern 1998, some of them 1999, but also later notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And when you say "later," are you talking about calendar years 2000/2001, in that era?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29
utterances.text: Yes, onwards, 2000, 2001. Even 2003 and 2004, there might be notes on those years as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How many pages of that notebook relate to 1998?
